A month ago, I was laid off.

I'd been at [Company] for [X years], and like a lot of people this year, I found out in a 15-minute call with someone from HR I'd never met. My access was gone before lunch.

I've had some time to sit with it, and here's what I've learned so far:

1. It's not a verdict on your worth. Layoffs are usually spreadsheet decisions. It took me about two weeks to actually believe this.

2. Your network is bigger than you think. I was blown away by how many people reached out: former colleagues, people I hadn't talked to in years, even strangers who'd been through the same thing.

3. Rest is productive. I spent the first week applying to everything in sight. It didn't help. Taking a few days to reset did.

4. Talk about it. I was embarrassed at first. But every time I told someone, I got a lead, an intro, or at least some perspective.

5. Get clear on what you actually want. This is an unexpected chance to ask whether I want my next role to look like my last one.

I'm now looking for my next role in [field/role]. If you know of a team that needs someone who [brief strength], I'd love to connect.

And if you've been laid off recently too, my DMs are open. You're not alone in this.

Most companies didn't get remote work wrong because remote work doesn't work. They got it wrong because they tried to run a remote company exactly like an office company, just over Zoom.

Same 9-to-5 hours. Same back-to-back meetings. Same expectation that you respond to Slack within four minutes, because that's the closest thing to someone being able to see you at your desk.

That's not remote work. That's an office with worse coffee.

The teams I've seen do it well changed a few things:

They write things down. Decisions, context, the reasoning behind a plan. If it only lives in a meeting, half the team never gets it.

They stopped measuring presence. Nobody cares if your green dot is on. They care whether the thing shipped.

They protect focus time. Fewer meetings, shorter meetings, and plenty of meetings replaced with a doc and a comment thread.

They meet up in person on purpose. A few times a year, for things that are actually better face to face, like planning, kickoffs, and getting to know each other. Not for sitting in a room on separate video calls.

None of this is complicated. It just requires managers to trust people and change their own habits, which is the hard part.

Curious what others have seen. What's one thing your company does that actually makes remote work work?

My first manager, [Name], did something in my second month that I still think about.

I'd made a mistake on a client report. Not a catastrophic one, but the numbers were wrong and the client noticed before we did. I was sure I was in trouble.

Instead she got on the call with the client and said, "We got this wrong, here's the corrected version, and here's what we're changing so it doesn't happen again." She never mentioned my name. Afterwards she sat down with me and walked through exactly where it went wrong and how to check for it next time. That was it. No lecture.

I didn't realize until years later how rare that is. A lot of managers take the credit when things go well and pass the blame down when they don't. She did the opposite, every time.

When I became a manager myself, I found out how hard that actually is. When your boss is asking what happened, it's really tempting to explain that it wasn't you. But I think about her a lot in those moments.

Your team will take risks and own their mistakes if they know you'll have their back in public and be honest with them in private. That's most of the job.

[Name], if you're reading this, thank you.

Everyone keeps asking whether AI will replace marketers. I think that's the wrong question.

What I'm actually seeing on our team is that AI has made the easy parts of marketing almost free. First drafts, ad variations, subject line testing, summarizing a pile of customer interviews. Stuff that used to take a junior marketer a day now takes twenty minutes.

Which sounds great, until you notice that your competitors have the same tools. When everyone can produce 50 blog posts a month, 50 blog posts a month stops being an advantage. The internet is filling up with content that's fine. Technically correct, well structured, and completely forgettable.

So the stuff that's getting more valuable is the stuff AI is bad at:

Knowing your customer better than anyone. Not persona slides, actual conversations.
Having a point of view. Saying something people might disagree with.
Taste. Knowing which of the 50 options is the good one, and why.
Distribution and relationships. People still trust people.

My guess is the marketers who do well over the next few years won't be the ones who use AI the most. They'll be the ones who use it to clear their plate so they can spend more time on the parts that require judgment.

I've been writing software for about [X] years now, and I've mentored a handful of junior devs along the way. Here are five things I wish someone had told me early on:

1. Read more code than you write. Open up the codebase and just read it. How do the senior people structure things? What do they name stuff? You'll learn more from that than from most tutorials.

2. Ask questions sooner. I used to spend a whole day stuck on something because I didn't want to look dumb. A 5-minute question would have saved me hours. Try for 30-60 minutes on your own, then ask. Nobody minds.

3. Learn to debug properly. Not just console.log everywhere (although, honestly, that works more often than people admit). Learn your debugger, read stack traces all the way through, and get comfortable reproducing a bug before you try to fix it.

4. Small PRs. Seriously. A 50-line PR gets a thoughtful review. A 2,000-line PR gets "LGTM."

5. Don't stress about the tech stack. Frameworks change every few years. Understanding how things work underneath (HTTP, databases, how memory works) sticks with you.

Bonus: write things down. Keep a doc of what you learned and what you shipped. Future you will thank you at review time.

Two years ago, I left a stable job to start [Company]. Last month, we shut it down.

I've started writing this post a few times and deleted it. It's not fun to talk about failing in public. But I've learned a lot, and I'd rather share it than pretend it didn't happen.

What went wrong:

We built too long before talking to customers. We spent our first eight months building something we thought people needed. When we finally launched, it turned out they had the problem, but not badly enough to pay for a solution.

We ran out of runway before we found product-market fit. By the time we figured out the right direction, we didn't have the money or the time to pursue it properly.

And honestly, I held on too long. There were signs a year in that I explained away because I didn't want to admit it wasn't working.

What I'd do differently:
• Sell before you build. Even a landing page and 20 conversations.
• Set clear milestones upfront for when to pivot or stop.
• Talk openly with your co-founder about how you're really feeling. We both had doubts and didn't say them out loud for months.

What I'm grateful for:
Our small team, who took a chance on us. Our early customers. Our investors, who were kind about it. And my family, who put up with a lot.

It still stings. But I don't regret trying.

I'm taking a few weeks to rest, then figuring out what's next. If you've been through something like this, I'd love to hear how you came out the other side.

A couple of years ago, I had a stretch where I'd sit in my car in the office parking lot for ten minutes every morning before I could make myself go inside.

I didn't tell anyone at work. I thought it would make me look weak, or like I couldn't handle the job. So I kept showing up, kept saying "busy but good!" when people asked, and kept getting worse.

What eventually helped was pretty ordinary. I told my manager I was struggling. She didn't make it weird. She asked what would help, we moved a deadline, and she reminded me we had an employee assistance program I'd completely forgotten about. I started seeing a therapist a few weeks later.

I'm sharing this because I think most workplaces use the right words about mental health now, but the day-to-day doesn't always match. A wellness webinar doesn't help much if everyone's still answering emails at 10pm and nobody feels safe saying "I'm not okay."

The things that actually made a difference for me:
Managers who ask how you're doing and actually wait for the answer.
Workloads that are realistic, instead of "resilience" training.
Leaders who talk about their own bad weeks.
Taking time off without having to justify it.

If you're in that parking lot right now, figuratively or literally, please tell someone. It gets a lot lighter once you're not carrying it alone.

Last week my laptop died two days before a big client presentation.

I called the manufacturer's support line expecting the usual: 45 minutes of hold music, three transfers, and a ticket number. Instead, the first person I spoke to, Marcus, listened to the whole story, said "Okay, let's make sure you have a working laptop before Thursday," and then actually did it. He arranged a replacement for next-day delivery and followed up by email that evening to confirm it had shipped.

The fix itself wasn't what stuck with me. It was that he cared more about my problem than about following the script.

It made me think about how we treat our own customers. A few takeaways:

🔹 Customers remember how you made them feel. Nobody remembers the return policy. They remember the person who helped.

🔹 Empower your front line. Marcus could make that call without escalating. Someone decided to trust their support staff that much.

🔹 Service is marketing. I've already told about ten people this story. That's worth more than any ad.

🔹 Follow-up builds trust. One short email turned a good experience into a great one.

Since then, I've been asking my team: where in our customer journey are we following the script when we should be solving the problem?

Unpopular opinion: hustle culture isn't making you more successful. It's making you more tired.

We've been sold the idea that 4 a.m. wake-ups, 80-hour weeks, and "sleep when you're dead" are the price of success. But look closer and a lot of the people preaching it are selling a course, a book, or a coaching program.

Here's what I've seen instead:

📉 Output doesn't scale with hours. Research has shown for years that productivity drops sharply past about 50 hours a week. Beyond that, you're mostly producing mistakes you'll fix later.

🧠 The best ideas need space. My best decisions didn't happen at my desk at 11 p.m. They happened on walks, in the shower, after a full night's sleep.

🔥 Burnout is expensive. Losing six months to burnout wipes out any gains from a year of grinding.

🎯 Busy isn't the same as effective. Hustle culture rewards looking busy. Real progress comes from working on the right things.

Working hard matters. Some seasons require more: a launch, a deadline, an early-stage startup. But "always on" isn't a strategy. It's a slow leak.

The goal isn't to work more. It's to work well, and still have a life worth working for.

Agree? Disagree? I'd love to hear where you land.

My newsletter just passed 10,000 subscribers. It took me about [two and a half years], and for most of that time growth was painfully slow, so I want to share what actually worked (and what didn't).

The first 1,000 took over a year. Mostly friends, coworkers, and people who found me through LinkedIn. I almost quit around subscriber 400.

What made a difference:

I picked a narrower topic. When I wrote about "marketing," nobody cared. When I started writing specifically about [B2B SaaS pricing], people started forwarding it, because it was the only place they could find that stuff.

I showed up every week, even when nobody seemed to be reading. Consistency was boring, but it mattered more than anything else.

I repurposed everything. Every issue turned into 2-3 LinkedIn posts. This was by far my biggest source of new subscribers.

I did a few swaps with other newsletter writers in adjacent niches. Each one brought in a few hundred people who actually stuck around.

What didn't work: paid ads (expensive, low-quality subscribers), giveaways (lots of signups, terrible open rates), and trying to go viral on Twitter.

Honestly, there was no single moment where it took off. It just slowly compounded until one month I noticed the numbers had picked up.

If you've been reading along, thank you. Seriously. And if you're thinking about starting one, just start. Your first issue will be bad. Mine was.

Networking tips for introverts (from an introvert who used to dread every event)

Networking doesn't have to mean working the room and collecting 50 business cards. Here's what's worked for me:

1️⃣ Go for depth, not breadth. Aim for two or three real conversations instead of meeting everyone. One genuine connection beats a dozen forgettable ones.

2️⃣ Arrive early. The room is quieter, people haven't settled into groups yet, and it's easier to start a conversation.

3️⃣ Prepare a few questions. "What are you working on that you're excited about?" works much better than "So, what do you do?"

4️⃣ Lean into listening. Introverts are often great listeners, and people remember how it felt to be heard.

5️⃣ Use one-on-ones. Coffee chats and video calls are often more comfortable, and more valuable, than big events.

6️⃣ Network online. Thoughtful comments, DMs, and sharing your work on LinkedIn count too.

7️⃣ Follow up. A short message after meeting someone ("Really enjoyed our chat about X") is where most relationships actually start.

8️⃣ Give yourself permission to leave. Set a goal, like two conversations, then head home and recharge. No guilt.

Networking is really just building relationships, and introverts tend to be very good at that.

Fellow introverts, what's worked for you? 👇

I spent seven years in sales before moving into [current role]. I didn't expect it to teach me much outside of work, but it ended up shaping how I deal with pretty much everything.

A few things that stuck:

You'll hear no a lot, and it's usually not about you. Early on, every rejection felt personal. After a few hundred of them, you realize most people are just busy, or it's the wrong time, or they don't have the budget. That's been useful well beyond cold calls.

Listening beats talking. My best deals happened when I shut up and let the customer tell me what was actually going on. Turns out this also works with your partner, your kids, and your friends.

Follow up. A lot of good things happen on the fourth email, not the first. People usually aren't ignoring you, they forgot. Same goes for job applications, favors, and friends you haven't seen in a while.

Ask for what you want. Sales trains you to ask for the close. I'm much better now at asking for a raise, asking for help, or just saying what I need.

Have a short memory. Bad call at 10am? You've got another one at 10:30. You don't get to carry it around all day.

I still don't love cold calling. But I'm grateful for the reps.

Today was my first day back at work after [six months] of parental leave.

I thought I'd be ready. I'd planned it all out: childcare sorted, bottles labeled, a list of what I'd missed at work. Then at drop-off this morning I sat in the car for a few minutes before I could drive away.

The day itself was fine, mostly. My laptop needed 47 updates. I've forgotten half my passwords. There's a new tool everyone uses that I've never heard of. And I kept checking my phone for updates from daycare, which, to be fair, they warned me about.

What I didn't expect was how nice it felt to just finish a thought without being interrupted. And to have adult conversations about something other than nap schedules.

A few things that made today easier, in case any managers or teams are reading:
My manager blocked my calendar for the first morning so I could catch up instead of jumping straight into meetings.
A teammate sent me a short "here's what changed" doc. Lifesaver.
Nobody said "must be nice to have had a vacation."

To any parent going back soon: it's okay to feel two things at once. I'm happy to be back and I miss my kid like crazy. Both are true.

Okay. Back to resetting passwords.

I think every product manager should learn some SQL. Not to become a data analyst, just enough to answer your own questions.

Here's why I started. A couple of years ago I wanted to know how many users had tried a feature more than once in their first week. Simple question. I filed a request with the data team and got an answer eight days later. By then we'd already made the decision based on a guess.

So I spent a few weekends learning the basics. SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, a couple of JOINs. That covered maybe 80% of what I needed.

What changed:

I stopped waiting. Most of my questions now take ten minutes, not a week.

I ask better questions. When you can poke at the data yourself, you notice weird things. "Why do half our signups on Tuesdays come from one country?" is not a question you'd ever think to file a ticket for.

The data team likes me more. When I do need their help, it's for something hard and interesting, not "can you count some rows for me."

I trust the numbers more, because I understand where they come from and what they leave out.

You don't need a course. Ask someone on your data team for read access and a few example queries, and start tweaking them. That's how most people I know learned.

PMs who already know SQL, did it change how you work?

A book that genuinely changed how I work: Deep Work by Cal Newport 📚

A few years ago, my days looked productive. Hundreds of Slack messages, back-to-back meetings, an inbox at zero. But at the end of the week, I'd struggle to name one meaningful thing I'd actually created.

Newport's argument hit hard: the ability to focus without distraction on cognitively demanding work is becoming rarer, and at the same time more valuable. Most of us spend our days on "shallow work," tasks that feel urgent but don't move the needle.

A few ideas that stuck with me:

🔹 Focus is a skill. It's like a muscle, and constant task-switching weakens it.

🔹 Schedule deep work like a meeting. If it's not on the calendar, it won't happen.

🔹 Embrace boredom. If you reach for your phone every time you're idle, your brain loses the ability to concentrate.

🔹 Be intentional about tools. Just because a tool has some benefit doesn't mean it's worth the cost to your attention.

What I changed:
✅ I block 2-3 hours every morning for focused work. No Slack, no email.
✅ I batch messages into set times during the day.
✅ I removed social apps from my phone's home screen.

The result? Fewer hours feeling busy, more hours actually getting things done.

If you're feeling stretched thin and still not making progress on what matters, I highly recommend this one.

Ten years ago this week, I started my first shift as a nurse. I was 23, terrified, and I triple-checked every med I gave that day.

I've been thinking about what's changed since then.

I've worked nights for longer than I've worked days. I've eaten more lunches standing up than sitting down. I've held hands with people on the worst day of their lives, and I've been there for some of the best ones too. I still remember the name of the first patient I lost.

Some things I know now that I didn't then:

The patient's family usually knows something's wrong before the monitors do. Listen to them.

The nurses who've been there 25 years have seen everything. Ask them. They were new once too.

You can't pour from an empty cup. I used to think that was just a poster in the break room. It isn't. I learned it the hard way around year four.

Kindness is a clinical skill. People heal better when they feel like someone sees them.

It's been a hard decade for healthcare, and a lot of good nurses have left. I get why. Some days I think about it too. But I'm still here, because on the good days there's nothing else I'd rather do.

To every nurse I've worked alongside: thank you for covering my patients when I needed a minute, for the 3am snacks, and for making the hardest job I know a little lighter.

Here's to the next ten.

After [X years] in recruiting and thousands of interviews, I can tell you the biggest mistake I see candidates make isn't a lack of experience.

It's failing to connect their experience to the job they're interviewing for.

So many talented people walk through everything they've done, every responsibility, every project, and leave it up to the interviewer to figure out why it matters. Most interviewers won't do that work for you.

Here's what that looks like:

❌ "In my last role, I managed the onboarding process for new clients."

✅ "In my last role, I rebuilt our client onboarding, which cut time-to-launch from six weeks to three. I know your team is scaling quickly, so I'd bring that same approach here."

Same experience. Completely different impact.

How to fix it:
1. Study the job description and identify the top 3 problems this role solves.
2. Pick stories from your experience that show you've solved similar problems.
3. Quantify results wherever you can.
4. Close the loop: tell them explicitly how it translates to their team.

Hiring managers aren't just asking "Can this person do the job?" They're asking "Can this person solve our problems?" Make it easy for them to say yes.

It took me way too long to learn how to say no at work.

For years I said yes to everything. Extra projects, last-minute favors, every meeting I was invited to. I thought that's what being a good teammate looked like. Mostly it meant I was doing a lot of things badly and working until 9 to keep up.

The turning point was pretty unglamorous. My manager asked why a project I actually cared about was three weeks behind, and the honest answer was that I'd said yes to so many small things there was no time left for it.

Some things that have helped me since:

"Let me check what I've got on and get back to you." It buys time instead of a reflexive yes.

"I can do this, but it means X will slip. Which is more important?" This puts the tradeoff back with the person asking, which is usually where it belongs.

"I'm not the right person for this, but [name] might be." Not every no has to be a dead end.

And sometimes just "No, I can't take that on right now." No long explanation needed.

The surprising part is how little pushback I've gotten. Most people respect a clear no way more than a yes that turns into something late and half-done.

I'm still working on it. But every no to something that doesn't matter is a yes to something that does.

A year ago I quit my in-house design job to go freelance. Here's what I learned, the good and the slightly painful.

Pricing is the hardest part. I undercharged my first five clients. Not by a little. I was so worried about losing work that I quoted numbers that made no sense once I added up the hours. I've raised my rates twice since and lost exactly one client because of it.

Contracts aren't optional. I learned this from a client who decided the logo was "basically done" and stopped replying. Now nothing starts without a signed contract and a 50% deposit.

Most of my work comes from people I already knew. Old coworkers, a friend of a friend, a former client who moved companies. Cold outreach got me almost nothing. Staying in touch got me most of my income.

Scope creep is real. "Can you just quickly…" is the most expensive phrase in freelancing. I now write down exactly what's included and what counts as an extra round.

Some months are slow, and that's normal. March was terrifying. May was so busy I barely slept. I keep a few months of expenses saved now so the slow months don't send me into a panic.

And the good part: I pick my projects, I work from wherever I want, and I've done some of the best work of my career this year.

If you're thinking about going freelance and want to chat, my DMs are open. Happy to share the contract template I wish I'd had.
